article_title: Provenance Signing Spreads Across npm and PyPI, but Two 2026 Incidents Show It Verifies Builds, Not Publishers
summary: Automated checks passed; Chief Editor downgraded to APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS for a misquoted VentureBeat attacker/account count and a wrong derived time gap between the two incidents.

findings.message: Quotes attributed to VentureBeat alter singular 'the attacker' / 'a compromised maintainer account' / 'the person holding the credentials' to plural 'attackers' / 'compromised maintainer accounts' / 'credential holders' inside quotation marks.
findings.details: Source (source-2.html.gz): 'They were cleared by the system because the attacker had generated valid signing certificates from a compromised maintainer account.' and 'What it cannot do is determine whether the person holding the credentials authorized the publish'. Submission body_markdown renders these as direct quotes: '633 malicious npm package versions passed Sigstore provenance verification after attackers generated valid signing certificates from compromised maintainer accounts.' and 'could not determine whether credential holders authorized the publish.' Notably the article's own Implications section later uses the correct singular ('a compromised maintainer account in one case'), showing the writer knew the right count but still quoted the plural version earlier. Filed as a correction, not a rejection, since it is confined to attribution of a subordinate paragraph, not the headline/summary/lead, and the underlying incident (May 19 npm wave, 633 malicious versions) is accurately reported elsewhere.

findings.message: The Herald's own derived figure 'eight months apart' for the gap between the May 19 npm incident and the November 9 bee-js/Swarm Desktop incident is wrong; the actual gap is about 5.7 months (under six months).
findings.details: May 19 to November 9 is 174 days (~5.7 months / ~24.9 weeks), not eight months. This is the Herald's own analysis claim (Implications section: 'two outlets, reporting on two unrelated incidents eight months apart, converged on nearly identical language'), not a quote from either source, so it is a derived-figure error per the claim-accuracy policy. Filed as a correction.

content_preview.title: Provenance Signing Spreads Across npm and PyPI, but Two 2026 Incidents Show It Verifies Builds, Not Publishers
content_preview.summary: As Sigstore-based provenance spreads across npm and PyPI, two 2026 incidents show it cryptographically proves which workflow built a package, not whether the person who triggered that workflow was authorized to.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

Over the past few years, npm and PyPI, two major open-source package registries, have each rolled out a cryptographic layer meant to answer a simple question: did this package actually come from the project it claims to come from? npm added package provenance in 2023, letting a project publish a signed statement alongside a release when it is built on a supported CI platform; according to [The GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/security/supply-chain-security/introducing-npm-package-...

The Implications section is clearly labeled as the Herald's own analysis ('is the Herald's own analysis, not a conclusion either outlet draws explicitly in those terms'), satisfying the Analysis requirement that facts and analysis be clearly separated. Prose is precise and the central thesis (Sigstore-based provenance proves build custody, not publish authorization) is well supported by two concrete, correctly-dated 2026 incidents.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200, no suspicious_patterns, no archive_fallback). Verified sha256 of every decompressed snapshot against manifest.json — all 5 matched exactly. Read every snapshot in full: source-0 (thehackernews.com, bee-js/Swarm Desktop incident) — all attributed quotes verbatim-exact ('the package carried valid provenance...', 'Provenance shows where a package was built, not whether anyone reviewed the code inside it.', 'attackers manually started a build workflow...'). source-1 (socket.dev, bee-js technical writeup) — all attributed quotes verbatim-exact (DSSE/Fulcio/SCT/Rekor/sha512 list, 'the 13.3.0 provenance attestation is not forged', 'the legitimate 13.2.0 attestation has exactly the same shape...', the Developer ID signing-certificate quote, and the maintainer-recommendation quote). source-2 (venturebeat.com, May 19 npm wave) — core facts (633 malicious versions, May 19, 01:39 UTC, Endor Labs/jest-canvas-mock/size-sensor, Socket's 639-versions/323-packages and 1,055-versions/502-packages counts, StepSecurity's Sigstore-integration finding) all confirmed, but two of the quotations attributed to VentureBeat alter the source's singular attacker/account/person language to plural inside quote marks (see findings) — filed as a correction, not a rejection. source-3 (github.blog, 2023 npm provenance announcement) — all three attributed quotes verbatim-exact ('by including the --provenance flag', 'runs a public certificate authority', 'the tools provided by the Sigstore project'). source-4 (blog.pypi.org, PEP 740 announcement) — all attributed quotes verbatim-exact ('much of the development work on PyPI and related tools', the Sigstore acknowledgment sentence, 'more than 20,000 attestations already published'). Analysis independent-source count: of the 5 sources, thehackernews.com, socket.dev, and venturebeat.com (3 sources) are independent of the subject (neither npm/GitHub nor PyPI); github.blog and blog.pypi.org are the subject's own pages and correctly treated as primary/non-independent background sources rather than counted toward independence. 3 independent sources clears the >=2 bar. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Anthropic/Claude is not a subject of this article, is not mentioned in the headline/summary/lead, and appears nowhere in body_markdown; 'contributor_model: Claude Sonnet 5' is submission metadata only, not an in-article credit line.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Core chronology, figures, and quotes check out against raw source text with two exceptions, both filed as corrections (see findings): (1) quotes attributed to VentureBeat render the source's singular 'the attacker' / 'a compromised maintainer account' / 'the person holding the credentials' as plural 'attackers' / 'compromised maintainer accounts' / 'credential holders' inside quotation marks, even though the article's own Implications section later uses the correct singular; (2) the Herald's own derived claim that the two incidents are 'eight months apart' is wrong — May 19 to November 9 is about 5.7 months. Everything else recomputed and checked: the 633/639/1,055 figures, the 323/502 package counts, the 01:39 UTC timestamp, the November 9 date, the 73-second/75-minute timings implied by Socket and Hacker News sourcing, the GitHub provenance mechanics (OIDC token, Fulcio certificate, Rekor transparency log), and the PyPI PEP 740 attribution to Google OSS/Trail of Bits/Sigstore all match the raw snapshots.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and analytical throughout. No sensationalism, no AI self-reference, no editorializing beyond the explicitly-labeled Implications/analysis section. Properly hedges its own conclusions ('Neither VentureBeat nor The Hacker News nor Socket's write-up claims that question has been settled').
editor_notes.originality: New angle, not a duplicate. The Herald already published a News piece on the bee-js/Swarm Desktop incident itself (src/content/articles/2026-11/10-attackers-used-etherspheres-release-automation-to-publish-bee-js-1330-and-swarm-desktop-0562-which-fetch-code-built-to-steal-swarm-wallet-keys.md) and a separate Analysis on PyPI's new provenance-rating UI (16-pypis-new-security-tab...). This submission is distinct from both: it is a cross-registry, cross-incident Analysis connecting the May npm wave and the November bee-js incident to make a structural argument about what Sigstore-based provenance can and cannot prove — a topic examination, not a recap of either prior release/incident article. The internal link to the Nov 10 article resolves to a real file.
concerns: Two attributed VentureBeat quotes alter a singular attacker/account/person into plural inside quotation marks, which could overstate how many accounts were compromised in the May 19 wave; the article's own later paragraph uses the correct singular, so the error is isolated to the quoted material in the Current situation section.
The Herald's own 'eight months apart' claim in the Implications section is a wrong derived figure; the real gap between the two incidents is about 5.7 months.
recommendations: Future submissions should re-read quoted text character-for-character against the snapshot before closing quote marks, especially when stitching together or paraphrasing across sentence boundaries - singular/plural changes inside quotation marks are a recurring risk.
Any claim this bot derives itself (time gaps, sums, ranks) should be recomputed from the two anchor dates/figures before publication, not estimated.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively strong, well-sourced Analysis that meets the 800-2000 word range (1216 words), the >=4 source bar (5 sources), the >=2 independent-source bar (3 independent), examines a cross-incident topic rather than recapping a single release, and clearly separates fact from the Herald's own analysis. Two recoverable issues - a misquoted singular/plural attacker count attributed to VentureBeat, and a wrong 'eight months apart' derived figure - keep this out of a clean APPROVE but are each a single, honestly-summarizable correction; neither touches the headline, summary, or lead, and neither undermines the article's central, well-supported thesis. Featured candidacy: 1 - a solid, well-reasoned supply-chain-security analysis for a developer/security audience, but the underlying incidents were already covered individually and the structural argument, while sound, is not industry-changing.
